Fake scam-help websites: how to check who is behind them

Before trusting a website that offers scam advice or recovery help, verify the organisation through a source independent of the page you are checking.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-08-14 · Updated 2026-09-25 · 5 min read

Quick answer: A familiar name, logo or secure connection does not prove a scam-help website is genuine. Check the organisation through an independently verified address before sharing details or paying. BeatTheScam’s guides are free. If you have already paid a suspicious service, contact your bank promptly and explain what happened.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

Correction — 25 September 2026

An earlier version of this guide said that BeatTheScam.com had been cloned. We have not substantiated that claim and have removed it. The guidance below concerns checking websites offering scam help; it does not report a verified impersonation incident involving BeatTheScam.

Start with the organisation, not the appearance

A website offering help with scams still needs checking. The FCA documents fraudulent communications and websites using its identity in its Fake FCA communications guidance. That is an example involving the FCA, not evidence that every advice website has been copied.

Find out who the service says it is and what it claims to do. An independent advice publisher, a regulator and a paid claims service have different roles. A logo or a claim to be “official” does not establish authority. If the page says another organisation endorses it, verify that through the named organisation's own contact details.

Check the address independently

Use a web address you already trust, such as a saved bookmark or an address obtained independently from the organisation. Do not rely on contact details supplied by the page or message you are trying to check.

BeatTheScam's website is https://beatthescam.com/. Its guides are free to read. A page demanding payment to unlock these guides is inconsistent with how this site provides them. A different site with a similar name is not automatically fraudulent; its identity and claims need their own checks.

Read the hostname in the address bar, not just words in the page title. HTTPS protects the connection but does not prove the operator is honest. Browser symbols vary, and an encrypted site can still be deceptive. Chromium explains the distinction in its An Update on the Lock Icon article.

Treat pressure and recovery promises as reasons to pause

Be cautious about an unexpected offer to recover money you have already lost, especially if it pressures you to pay before you can check it. Do not install software at an unverified service's request or give it banking passwords.

A fee is not, on its own, proof of a scam. The FCA explains in its Using claims management companies guidance that some genuine claims services charge for their work. Check the provider, service and terms independently before deciding. An apparent recovery offer deserves more scrutiny than its own testimonials or promises. See our recovery scam warning signs for that specific situation; the FCA also describes recovery room scams.

Heed browser security warnings. The absence of a warning is not confirmation that a website is safe. Chrome Help describes its warnings about unsafe sites.

If you have already used the website

Stop sending information or money while you check what happened. The NCSC gives different phishing recovery advice depending on what you shared or installed.

  • Only viewed it: if you entered nothing and downloaded or installed nothing, the NCSC says further action is unlikely to be needed; remain alert to unusual account activity.
  • Shared a password: change it on the genuine service and on other accounts where you reused it.
  • Shared banking or card details or paid: contact your bank or card issuer promptly using a trusted channel. Ask how to secure the account and what payment-recovery options apply.
  • Installed software or suspect device compromise: follow the NCSC’s device-recovery guidance; do not follow more instructions from the suspect service.

Keep messages, receipts and the address you already have. Do not return to an unsafe page solely to gather a screenshot.

Report concerns through the right route

Report a suspicious website through the NCSC website-reporting form. A report asks for assessment; it is not a declaration that an offence has been proved. You can also notify an organisation whose identity appears to have been used through independently verified contact details.

For suspected fraud, use the police reporting route for your nation in this guide’s reporting panel. It distinguishes Scotland from England, Wales and Northern Ireland and gives the appropriate contacts. If you have lost money, contact your bank as well.

Frequently asked questions

Has BeatTheScam.com been impersonated?

We have not substantiated the claim in the earlier version of this guide. We have corrected it rather than treating it as a documented incident. This does not establish that impersonation has never happened. If you encounter a suspicious page, verify its claims independently and use the reporting routes above.

Does asking for payment prove a scam-help website is fake?

No. BeatTheScam's guides are free, but some genuine services charge fees. Verify the provider and purpose of the charge. Pressure to pay before you can check is a reason to stop and investigate, not a substitute for evidence about the provider. The FCA explains paid claims services in its Using claims management companies guidance.

Can I get back money paid to a suspicious service?

Ask your bank or card issuer promptly. Options depend on how you paid and the circumstances. The Payment Systems Regulator says eligible UK-to-UK Faster Payments or CHAPS transfers made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall under mandatory APP reimbursement rules. Eligibility, time limits and other conditions apply; a refund is not guaranteed.

Should I pay for identity protection after visiting a suspicious page?

Simply viewing a page does not establish identity theft. If personal details may be misused, consider whether Cifas Protective Registration suits the risk. Cifas currently lists a £30 fee for two years; the service prompts extra identity checks by participating organisations. It does not recover money or guarantee fraud prevention.

Fast checks

  • Pause before sending money or credentials
  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
